purpose: Letrozole is most commonly used to treat certain types of breast cancer in women who have gone through menopause. It works by lowering estrogen levels in the body, which helps slow or stop the growth of hormone-sensitive breast cancers. It may also be used off-label to help with fertility treatments.
how_it_works: Your body makes a small amount of estrogen even after menopause, partly through a process involving an enzyme called aromatase. Letrozole blocks that enzyme, which reduces the amount of estrogen your body produces. Since some breast cancers need estrogen to grow, lowering estrogen levels helps slow or stop the cancer.
common_side_effects: Hot flashes, night sweats, joint or muscle aches and stiffness, fatigue or tiredness, headaches, dizziness, nausea, bone loss over time, and increased cholesterol levels. Some women also notice hair thinning or mild swelling in the hands and feet.
warnings: Letrozole can weaken your bones over time, increasing the risk of osteoporosis and fractures, so your doctor may monitor your bone density. Do NOT take this medication if you are pregnant or could become pregnant, as it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, especially estrogen-containing products, as they can reduce how well letrozole works. Contact your doctor if you notice unusual bone pain, vision changes, or signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is one 2.5 mg tablet taken by mouth once a day, with or without food. Try to take it at the same time each day. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed one and continue your regular schedule. Never take two doses at once.
